name: Yaygir
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Crowley, Terry. 1979. Yaygir. In R.M.W. Dixon & Barry J. Blake (eds.), Handbook of Australian Languages, Vol. 1, 363-384. Canberra: Australian National University Press (open-access digitisation, ANU Open Research hdl:1885/114846; co-edition Amsterdam: John Benjamins, doi:10.1075/z.hal1.09cro).
catalog_locator: p. 369, section 2.1 'Phonemes and their realizations', last paragraph before 2.2 Phonotactics (of the ANU scan; page offset +16)
catalog_quote: Primary stress in Yaygir is placed on the initial syllable of a word when there are no long vowels, otherwise the first long vowel is stressed, e.g. /ya:laɲ/ 'tongue' [yá:laɲ] /iba/ 'back' [íppa] /ŋagar/ 'chest' [ŋákkar] /una:ŋay/ 'excrement' [uná:ŋɛy] /warɖu:ri/ 'shin' [warʈú:ri] /duguburuɲ/ 'locust' [dúguburuɲ] ... [same page, two paragraphs earlier:] Any single consonant or semi-vowel following a stressed short vowel is obligatorily geminated in Yaygir. This is particularly noticeable with the stops and the nasals but it also applies to the lateral and rhotic phonemes, as well as the semi-vowels (when the latter either become pre-stopped or fricativized, as mentioned above).
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: matches) and re-extracted PDF page 385 with extracted text; the header reads '2.1 Phonemes and their realizations 369', confirming the +16 offset. The passage is there verbatim: 'Primary stress in Yaygir is placed on the initial syllable of a word when there are no long vowels, otherwise the first long vowel is stressed, e.g.' followed by the six examples, and two paragraphs earlier 'Any single consonant or semi-vowel following a stressed short vowel is obligatorily geminated in Yaygir.' I also viewed the page scan : the phonetic forms in the compilers quote ([yá:laɲ], [íppa], [ŋákkar], [uná:ŋɛy], [warʈú:ri], [dúguburuɲ]) match the printed page (the scanned text garbles them; the compilers…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress goes to the first long vowel in the word; if the word has no long vowel, it falls on the initial syllable. Long vowels are the only heavy syllables that attract stress (Crowley gives no vowel+semivowel weight rule of the Gumbaynggir kind). A single consonant after a stressed short vowel is phonetically geminated.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned anywhere in the chapter (the only stress passages in pp. 363-390 are the two sentences quoted).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Caveat from the source itself (pp. 363, 365): the whole sketch rests on a few days' elicitation in January 1973 from one non-fluent last speaker, Mr Sandy Cameron of Yamba, and 'the facts could never be checked and the gaps filled'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level: 'the initial syllable of a word'. Examples are isolated citation forms with phonetic transcriptions; no phrase-level statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Crowley 1979 describes Yaygir (his spelling; Morelli/Muurrbay 'Yaygirr', AIATSIS E10, ISO xya) = Glottolog yayg1236, as recorded from its last speaker, Sandy Cameron of Yamba, in January 1973; no dialect is named. The earlier scan marked the source 'unreachable' via the Benjamins DOI, but the 1979 ANU Press printing is open access at the ANU Open Research repository (hdl:1885/114846, bitstream), which is the copy used here.
